notes.claim: To compare fractions with unlike denominators, find equivalent fractions for both so that they share the same denominator.
When fractions have the same numerators, the one with the greater denominator is smaller.
Multiplying the top and bottom of each fraction by the denominator of the other gives a common denominator and keeps each fraction's value the same.
Comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole.
Judging fractions by their whole numbers (1/5 greater than 1/2 because 5 is greater than 2) is a documented misconception.
Unit fractions can be compared and ordered by looking at the denominator: the greater the denominator, the smaller the fraction.
When fractions have the same numerators, the denominators are compared, and the greater denominator gives the smaller fraction.
A common misconception is to compare fractions by whole-number size, judging 1/5 greater than 1/2 because 5 is greater than 2; researchers call this whole-number bias.
The denominator says how many equal parts the whole is divided into, so a bigger denominator means the whole has been cut into more pieces.
